title: Optics and Photonics: A Practical Reference
lede: Photonics is the layer underneath half the technology in the other sheets: the LiDAR on a robot, the lithography that makes a chip, the fiber under the ocean, the transceiver in a rack. This guide catalogs {{N_ENTRIES}} devices across seven classes, organized the way an optical system is actually specified, by wavelength first and everything else second.

facets.label: Wavelength
facets.tip: Spectral band the device works in. UV under 400 nm · Visible 400–700 nm · NIR 700–1,100 nm, where silicon still detects · SWIR 1.1–2.5 um, the telecom and eye-safe region · MWIR 3–5 um and LWIR 8–14 um, the two atmospheric windows thermal imaging uses · THz below that. Most devices span a band, and the material sets where it ends.

facets.label: Used in
facets.tip: Markets where the device is a normal choice rather than an exotic one. Most photonics parts serve several, which is why a component designed for telecom volume often turns up in a sensor.

facets.label: Form factor
facets.tip: How the device arrives. Chip = a die or wafer-level part · Component = a discrete packaged optic or emitter · Module = a packaged subsystem with drive electronics · Instrument = a benchtop or rack system. Form factor usually predicts cost and volume better than the physics does.

facets.label: Unit cost
facets.tip: Rough price for one unit at the quality a working system needs, not the cheapest catalog part. Photonics spans six orders of magnitude here, and the same function can sit at either end depending on wavelength and specification.

facets.label: Maturity
facets.tip: Mature = commodity, many suppliers, decades of use · Established = commercial with a solid supply base · Emerging = shipping but still improving quickly · Early = research and first products.
